title: From APIs to MCP: Enterprise Governance, Registry, and Controls

segments.text: All right, hello. Uh thank you for joining me today this late afternoon on a Friday. I saw some early talks as as well about
MCP. So, the afternoon's packed with MCP. I'm trying to give a little bit of a different perspective uh into the topic today. So, my name is Stefan. I'm platform
experience lead at Deutsche Bank uh working on the Copper Bank uh data platforms that we have. So, basically we have um we are centralized team.
We provide the API platform for the organization. And then we have decentralized in the organization multiple teams providing um APIs uh on our platform
for both internal as well as external consumption. Let's get started uh with my only slide about API today. Um as you can see um or maybe you remember um from the
past APIs have changed the way that system uh integrate with each other. Um in the past um in the in my early career when we would integrate two systems, we
would establish a project. And um there would be a consuming team that would define the the the interface definition. The provider would uh create
the interface. And next time we have a new project, we need a new interface. With APIs this has significantly changed. Not only because APIs, but
because we learned to develop um APIs that are for reuse. So, the APIs they are sitting on top of multiple systems and they are offering
these enterprise capabilities in a standardized way. And every time I now have a new project, I can just reuse them. Now, as the world is shifting um from um
the way we are integrating systems. APIs are seen as good but not sufficient. So, agents integrate with tools and with capabilities in a different way.
And they also want a standardized way for that. API is not offering this. We have multiple different types of APIs. We have REST APIs, we have GraphQL,
GRPC. And the idea here is that while a provider is providing this API for use, the consumer has to adapt and has to talk
all these different dialects. With MCP, the new newly introduced protocol, which you may be aware of, um this thing is changing and now the
the the complexity of the integration is no longer on the consumer side or on the agent side, but it's on the provider side. So, the provider is providing
a unified interface for the agents and um the agents can simply consume them. How this would look like is more or less like this. Uh we have uh again our
systems on the bottom. We can also have our APIs and MCP would come on top. Kind of an MCP layer. It's not necessarily a
layer. This may be multiple um MCP servers and tools and the agent would consume from it. The idea here is as you can see, the interface is always
looking the same from a protocol perspective. I'm sure many of you have already explored um MCP, but if you have not, uh this is a little bit very high level how
MCP would work. On the one hand, I have the discoverability layer or the discoverability view where I call the list of tools and I receive them and in a very similar
way I can just invoke the capability. So, it's not difficult at all for the agents to integrate with this MCP. And MCP is becoming more and more
um popular. So, it's was released 18 months ago, I guess, uh November 2024. And I actually tried to find out how many MCP servers we have out there. I
have found um different registries, public registries, four or five. They have somewhere around 10 to 15,000 um um MCP servers published. But, um I thought that I scan GitHub.
So, I asked my favorite AI to look up for me, and this is the number that I have received. So, back in the end of
June, we had around uh 12 19,000 um repositories flagged as MCP server on MCP. >> [cheering] >> Now, if you do this query more
regularly, you're going to see that the number is increasing. So, we have roughly per month an increase of 1,000 APIs, which match a a little bit with
when MCP was initially um published. Studies have shown though that um many of the repositories and the servers that are published, they are invalid.
They are abandoned. They are only placeholder. Only appear to be 50% of them. 22% of them have been inactive for more than 1 year.
And that's the challenge that we have uh when we are looking into enterprise. Uh we are in Deutsche Bank, we have our teams also adopting uh MCP,
and they are doing POCs. They are trying it out. Uh and we don't have the visibility what is going on. Let's have a look into this one picture
right here. As you can see, we have here um multiple three agents connecting to multiple different tools. And this all looks good in the
beginning, but if you look carefully, you're going to see that the customer data server is duplicated. So, we have two different servers published there
and um two different agents consuming it. We have on the top, we have the investment server, not discoverable at all, nobody's aware of it. And we have here in the middle
something that looks more like a POC or a developer trying out something. So, the um that that's the that's the problem that um without a governance, um
we um we start to see those MCP servers everywhere and we um we simply do not have visibility about them. Now, this comes to our first takeaway in
Deutsche Bank, how we are handling it and we are implementing and introducing a uh internal MCP registry. With the MCP registry, all the servers
that we have are published. They now uh receive a owner. We have a visibility of the exposed tools, uh the connected systems, so which um
agents are consuming them or maybe which subsequent systems they have. Very important, we have the data classification and we have the life cycle stage. So, we
are now aware that that one server we saw before, uh that MCP underline server, is actually only in development. It's actually only a draft.
Now, while before uh we had scattered servers without a single source of truth, after we have had registered those servers on the MCP registry, I'm
now actually able to govern everything. I have clear visibility of the ownership of those servers. So, if something happens, I know how to who to contact. I
have full transparency, and I can start to enforce controls. Now, let's assume we have introduced our MCP registry. As you can see on this picture, the
problem we had before is solved. Customer data has been consolidated. Some architect did some good work. Investment server is still there. It's not being consumed,
but we have transparency of it. And that one POC has been now decommissioned. So, this looks good. And now, this is the challenge that we
have in a um enterprise environment. What we start to see, if we look closely, is that the connectivity between the agent and the workflows server has performance
issues. Between the agent and customer data, we actually have a security issue. So, this server is not very well secure. Authentication not happening properly.
Market data server is a little bit unstable. And account balance, it's increasing its usage. These are typical things that we see within our environment. We have seen
this before in APIs, and we will start to see this also with MCP. And here comes our big big takeaway number two. We are building on top of
our API strategy. We introduce an API platform in in between between the server and the agent. So, now the agent, when wants to consume the server, will connect to the
API platform. Will perform the tool call, and will receive an approved access to enterprise capabilities, such as customer data, workflow, etc. And the nice thing here is that you can
start to enforce, um, controls on the gateway. It may be security and authentication to ensure, um, a good, um, integration with that server. It may be traffic
control. Traffic control could be load balancing. It could also be throttling and rate limiting. With we can we have a centralized place where we can introduce threat
protection, like, for example, prompt injection, uh, or tool call amplification, which is when an agent starts to consume multiple tools, um, multiple times. We have a very high
number of transactions. And which what is very important for enterprise scale, uh, logging and audit. We start to have with the API platform, we have a
centralized, uh, place to, um, monitor who has accessed what and when. And actually, this is not different at all from our, um, API strategy. So, this
is our API governance blueprint that we had. We have the centralized gateway in the middle offering security and authentication, which we have discussed about, but we also have this as a
decoupling layer, which is what I find quite interesting. Decoupling layer means that the agent or the consumer is consuming the API from the gateway.
It doesn't know where the API or the server is actually hosted. So, if I want to rehost my API, I can do this easily
without have having to change my integration because my consumer consumes the gateway. We talked about throttling and rate limiting, um, and load balancing resilience, uh, very important two
topics, and response caching. Response caching is one of the answers that I give when people ask, um, sh- if I use an API gateway, I actually
have a bottleneck. I have a single point of failure. And the API gateway is adding an additional hop and is also adding latency. Yes, it does add a few
milliseconds of latency, but if everything is well designed and well implemented uh with uh response caching, I not only provide a faster answer where possible,
but I also reduce costs because my transactions no longer going to my cloud provider in the back end and I don't have to pay the transactions
anymore. We have talked about analytics and monitoring, a centralized catalog, which was our um takeaway number one, and uh I can actually start to implement
standards. Now, let's think of it. Um we are in Deutsche Bank doing the um our API journey for many years now, uh more or less 10 years.
We have already many hundreds and thousands of APIs that have published internally. Probably for all the different capabilities, we have an API already. So, I have an existing API exposure. We
have invested a lot of time in learning how to define this API, how to define the different controls for throttling, for rate limiting, et cetera.
Now, somebody um we are all um being asked to deliver MCP services. So, the obvious thing to do is that I will add a
new native MCP exposure. So, my customer data um capability that I had before with API, and now it's obvious, I offer this with MCP. Now, there are some other talks
here today or there were describing that also with MCP, uh the design is actually significantly different, but uh we are not going to the design specifically. Uh
we are we are talking about an API or a capability being exposed in more or less similar way as MCP capability just because agents integrate this in a
better way. So, this has a risk. I have to integrate all my controls, implement all my controls again. Everything that I did before with my API, I have to do again for my
MCP. And this introduces control gaps. My rate limiting, um, my throttling that I have implemented before, I have to do again. And I may do this differently,
which is a risk for my back end. I have a version drift. My customer data API is already version two, and I forgot to update MCP, or probably vice versa
because the API is older, I'm now investing on my MCP server, and I forget about the API. So, my API consumers, the consumers of this
capability, are now having a outdated, uh functionality. I have, um, ownership split. Who owns the MCP server, and who owns the API? I don't
know. This may be the same team, may not. It's a confusion in the organization, and and the evidence is spread. Now, the evidence of who has consumed this
capability is spread in multiple servers, difficult to follow up on issues, or when there is an audit, for example. And we are working with our IT partners
to offer a solution for that. Imagine this is my, um, my existing integration. I have my traditional API client, online banking, mobile banking, whatever that is, it's
consuming my API proxy. This API proxy is already well designed, is well defined, has authentication, quota, rate limiting, et cetera, and routes the traffic to my existing
API implementation. That's how we have have done API for so long. What is now actually possible is that instead of me doing the obvious
thing, that is to create either a new API implementation or a new MCP server implementation in back end offering the same capability or just creating a proxy that um
routes the API, I can do everything within the API platform. My traditional um API client consumes the proxy. But my agent consumes an MCP proxy that
is wrapping the API proxy. What I gain here is that all these controls are not duplicated. Everything stays the same. Yes, I may want to have
more granular or different controls on top of my MCP server. Maybe my rate limiting will be yet uh another one because I want to have something
more authentic. I can do this, but I can still rely on this on this foundation from my API proxy that I have built for
so long. And here's how we are doing this in general. Our MCP blueprint looks um has three different layers. Layer number one will be registration only.
Registration only is if you really have a very strong use case not to be um on the on a centralized gateway or maybe uh you have a SaaS application
or whatever and you don't need to use the gateway, you register so that we have control, we have visibility of what is out there.
If you are really um just starting the MCP journey and you just want to offer the capability in a MCP format, but you're not doing the whole design of
your of your server of your capability from scratch. You're building more or less the same. Generate this from your API. So, um for fast adoption um
or this early adoption, uh we are asking our teams to reuse what has been there already, the existing APIs, uh reusing the contracts, authentication, and monitoring by
wrapping the uh the existing API proxy. However, if you really have an advanced team uh has been the journey for so long cannot be so long, right? Maximum um
18 months, but you have an advanced team um that um wants to really build an MCP server well designed, you can do this, but still
publish this in the API platform to have this centralized and controlled governance. After all, this is how on a very high level our architecture
uh is looking like. My agent proxy is exposed also on the API platform. My application or my agentic application consumes this proxy that routes the traffic to the to the
runtime. The agent runtime can then decide um I may want to consume another LLM uh or any LLM or maybe I want to consume a MCP
server. I would not do this directly. The agent will go back to the API platform and uh the API platform will reroute this to the to the back-end
implementation. As you can see, the API platform continues to be a centralized um component of our architecture managing um all the integrations with our applications that we have.
Wrapping up um we want to be visible by registry, controlled by gateway, and scale through uh API reuse. So, initially we just register everything
so that we know that it actually exists. I know the owner, I know the tools, the systems, and I have the life cycle. I introduce runtime controls, but not
everything separately. I introduce those controls in a centralized managed API gateway. I try to reuse APIs building on the existing governance that I have.
I have three different adoption patterns that we're offering based on the risk, as we have discussed before. And the most important thing that we're telling the organization is
to keep this enterprise mindset. We want to treat all the tools as capabilities. Don't treat them differently, treat them as we have learned how to treat APIs,
capabilities that are well exposed and well managed with every MCP server becoming part of our enterprise control surface. Thank you very much. >> Thank you, Stefan. Thank you.
So, I have one question as someone that I don't work in such big in scale organization, but what is your advice to the people that
want to use MCP and want to sell the idea of MCP to the management? Why we should buy this? >> That's a very good question. That's a
question that I was trying to answer also during this whole conference. Um, MCP is a topic that is all over the place, and I honestly believe that if you're just
building another API, you should actually I mean, if the organization wants this, we have the solution, right? But you should probably not do this.
You'll build an MCP server if you really have an a new native AI integration. Um your agent wants to I mean your new use case is really
agentic. You don't have this implementation before. You don't have this in a as an API before. Then you build this with an MCP server. That's
the answer that I have received so far. But same as all of us, I guess, I'm also learning this topic at the moment. >> Nice. And
the other one which I have is Um let's say that we adopted them MCP idea. Um is there any difference in the maintenance cost between maintaining
just regular API and MCP server? Is it more costly in terms of developer time? Or yeah, I don't know. Did >> I I don't know.
I don't know how to answer that. Is it more costly? Probably it's going to be different. It's going to be a different cost. Probably if
you're building a new MCP server, you're doing this in an agentic way. The API you had a team of 10 people implementing it. Your MCP server will be probably
implemented by some co-pilot. Is it more expensive or not? I don't know how many tokens we are consuming. So, difficult question. >> So, it it depends on our Anthropic
subscription. >> Exactly. >> [laughter] >> Thank you. Thank you. >> Thank you very much. >> time. Thank you, Stephen.
